common_name: De Barao Tomato (Brazilian-Russian Heirloom Paste Tomato)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set out sturdy, hardened-off transplants once nights stay reliably above 50F.

directions: De Barao is a long-vined indeterminate heirloom grown widely across Russia, Ukraine, and Brazil for its heavy, reliable yields of small, egg-shaped paste tomatoes. Set transplants against a tall stake, trellis, or cage, since the vines keep climbing and fruiting right up until frost. The compact two- to three-ounce fruits hold their shape well, cracking less than many plum types, which makes them popular for canning, drying, and sauce. Keep soil moisture even through fruit set to avoid blossom-end rot, and prune lower foliage for airflow in humid climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant promptly once danger of frost passes, since this variety's main advantage is a short, early season.

directions: Latah was bred at the University of Idaho to give gardeners in the state's short, cool-summer growing regions a dependable early harvest, and it has been passed along by seed savers since it first appeared in exchange listings in the early 1980s. The compact determinate bush stays tidy enough for a cage or short stake and sets its crop of small, bright red, sweet-flavored fruit earlier than most other open-pollinated tomatoes. Because the plant matures and ripens quickly, it suits northern gardens, high-elevation sites, and anywhere a reliable early tomato is wanted before the main crop comes in. Keep watering consistent through the compressed fruiting window to get the best flavor and size from the small fruits.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and set out promptly, since this dwarf variety is bred to ripen quickly in short, cool seasons.

directions: Alpatieva 905 A is a mid-20th-century Russian heirloom bred for fast, reliable production from a notably compact, almost dwarf-sized determinate plant only about two feet tall. Despite its small stature it carries a heavy set of two- to three-ounce, globe-shaped red fruit with a good, old-fashioned tomato flavor, making a single stake or small cage sufficient support. Its short stature and early ripening suit container growing, raised beds, and cold-climate gardens where a long season isn't available. Water evenly and harvest promptly as fruit colors up, since the small plant can only carry a limited load of ripening tomatoes at once.

common_name: Ukrainian Purple Tomato (Purple Russian Heirloom Plum)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed, giving the long vines a tall support from the start.

directions: Ukrainian Purple, also sold as Purple Russian, is an indeterminate heirloom valued for its elongated plum-shaped fruit that ripens to a deep, dusky purple-brown often tinged with green near the shoulders. The rich, sweet-tart flesh is meaty and relatively low in juice, so the fruit holds together well in sauces and salsas while still tasting good eaten fresh. It stays productive later into cool fall weather than many heirlooms, tolerating temperatures that would stop lighter-fruited varieties. Stake or cage the vigorous vine early and keep watering consistent to limit cracking on the thin-skinned fruit as it ripens.
